lesson: Dark tints below #444444 blend into the dark page background (#222) and make parts hard to distinguish. Because tint MULTIPLIES with the sprite art rather than replacing it, the effective threshold is higher on already-dark art: on a dark (brown) body_E, tint #5a4a6a and even #6b5c82 both rendered near-invisible against the backdrop; #b39ddb was the first value that read clearly. On dark bodies keep every tint channel well above #44, or start from a lighter base color (blue/green/yellow) if you want a saturated hue.

STYLE BRIEF — "ABYSSAL LANTERN". A house style for deep-sea lantern-creatures: a dim cool-cored body that carries all of its light out at the extremities. Apply all four principles together; they are what make separate monsters read as one family.

(1) VALUE SPLIT — dim core, near-white lit tips. Fixed 4-tint palette: body tint #4a5a8c (deep indigo), arms and legs tint #5f7a9b (slate-teal), antennas tint #ffe9a3 (lantern amber), eyes tint #b8f2e6 (pale cyan). Core parts stay inside the 0x4a-0x9b per-channel band; lit parts stay above 0xb8 on every channel. Rule: never give two touching parts tints within 0x30 per channel of each other — the value gap is what makes the tips read as emitting light. Build on a light base color (blue/green/yellow) rather than dark, since tint multiplies (see the dark-tint lesson above).

(2) TAPER DOWNWARD — bulb on stalks. Scale descends head to foot: antennas scale 1.15, body scale 1.0, arms scale 0.8, legs scale 0.65 plus dy 10 (the leg shrink opens a gap at the default leg offset y:100, and dy 10 closes it). The silhouette must always be top-heavy.

(3) SYMMETRIC SPLAY, EXACTLY ONE ASYMMETRIC TELL. Arms angle 14, legs angle -8: because applyStyle negates angle on the mirrored side of a pair, these read as an outward flare, never as a tilt. Then break symmetry exactly once — antennas are NOT placed as a mirrored pair, so add_antennas with count 2 and dx -16 slides the whole 50px-spaced cluster off-center to the left. One off-axis element per monster, never two.

(4) WIDE EYE BAND OVER A SMALL LOW MOUTH. Odd eye counts only: count 3, scale 0.55, dy -10 (eye spacing is 40, so three eyes span 80px as a band across the upper face). Mouth pulled down and pinched: scaleX 0.7, scaleY 0.8, dy 16. Restrict eye styles to light-valued ones (cute_light, psycho_light, blue) so the eyes look lit from within rather than painted on; avoid dead and cute_dark, which kill the glow.

Tint values are NOT comparable across parts, and tint can only ever darken — so the ABYSSAL LANTERN "fixed 4-tint palette" cannot be trusted as written. Evidence from the body_E build: arms tinted #5f7a9b (numerically LIGHTER) rendered darker and duller than a body tinted #4a5a8c, because tint multiplies against each sprite's own base art and body_blueE starts from different channel values than arm_blueA. Likewise antennas tinted #ffe9a3 over yellow art rendered saturated ORANGE, not near-white amber, so the lit-tip glow never appeared. Two consequences: (a) the brief's rule "never give two touching parts tints within 0x30 per channel" is unenforceable by comparing tint numbers — judge the value gap from a screenshot instead; (b) the brief's own palette breaks that rule anyway (body #4a5a8c vs arms #5f7a9b differ by only 0x15/0x20/0x0f). To actually get near-white lit tips, pass NO tint (or a very faint one) on the lightest base color available — a "bright" tint still darkens.

This MCP server exposes only four build tools — create_body, add_eyes, add_arms, add_antennas. There is NO add_legs, add_mouth, or clear_monster tool, even though scene.js implements all three. Do not plan a build around legs or a mouth: two ABYSSAL LANTERN principles depend on them and must be re-expressed. (a) To clear the canvas, just call create_body — it calls clearMonster() internally and replaces the whole monster. (b) For principle 2's top-heavy taper, the "legs scale 0.65 + dy 10" step is impossible, and body_E is widest at the BOTTOM, so it lands bottom-heavy; get the taper from the body itself instead — try create_body shape E with scaleY around 0.85 and a scaleX taper, or use shape C/D, rather than relying on shrinking legs. (c) Principle 4's "small low mouth" is unachievable, which leaves the lower body empty on tall shapes — keep the eye band nearer the vertical middle (dy 0 to +10 rather than -10) so the face doesn't float at the top of a blank mass.

The antenna sprite's STALK is dark brown in the source art for every color variant, and tint can only darken — so a stalk can never be lightened. Untinting antennas (the lesson-#3 trick for bright tips) gives a bright bulb on a near-invisible stalk against the #2d2d44 canvas, so the bulbs read as detached floating dots and the ABYSSAL LANTERN idea of "light carried out along a limb" is unachievable at the stalk. Plan for antennas as floating bulbs and keep them tucked near the body silhouette. Concrete tradeoff measured on round body_B with eyes at dy 5: add_antennas dy -25 does clear the stalk bases off the eye band (fixing the earlier collision) but pushes the bulbs far enough out that they float free — dy -15 is the better compromise, clearing the eyes while keeping the bulbs visually attached.

Eye scale decides whether the wide eye band reads as eyes or as one solid bar, because eye spacing is a fixed 40px. At count 3 + scale 0.65 the sprites overlap and their whites merge into a continuous white rectangle that reads as a visor or mouth-grille, not three eyes — keep scale at 0.5-0.55 so visible gaps remain between them. Separately, watch the brightness hierarchy: untinted psycho_light eyes render pure white and out-shine untinted yellow antenna bulbs (saturated orange, lower luminance), which inverts the lantern read by making the face — not the tips — the brightest thing on the canvas. If the antennas are meant to be the light source, either use cute_light or knock the eyes down with a faint tint around #cfe8e0 so they sit just below the bulbs in value.

Part attachment offsets in parts.js are ABSOLUTE pixel values and do NOT scale with the body's scale param — so any create_body scale below 1 detaches the limbs. Measured on body_B: at scale 1.0 its radius is about 113px, at scale 0.88 about 99px, so each side's edge moves ~14px inward while arms stay at their fixed offset; the arms' own scale (0.7) additionally pulls their inner edge outward, widening the gap further. Passing dx -10 to add_arms was visibly too little and left floating arms on both sides. Rule: when shrinking the body, compensate arms with dx of roughly -(bodyRadius x (1 - bodyScale)) and then some for the arm's own shrink — for body_B scale 0.88 with arms scale 0.7 use about dx -22, not -10. The same absolute-offset problem applies to eyes and antennas, so re-check the face and the antenna bases in a screenshot whenever body scale is not 1.

Use arm pose A, not pose B, for the ABYSSAL LANTERN splay. Pose B renders as thin near-vertical strands beside the body, and on a near-vertical shape the angle 14 flare from principle 3 reads as a slight tilt instead of an outward splay — pose A's curved arms make the same 14 degrees legible as a flare. Pose B was tried specifically to stop the arms adding mass low on the body and it did NOT help: mass distribution was unchanged, so it cost splay legibility for nothing. Broader conclusion from three builds: principle 2's top-heavy silhouette is structurally unreachable on this server, because with no add_legs the body IS the whole silhouette and sits centered. Stop spending iterations on arm pose or arm scale to fix taper — the only lever that moves it is the body-scale-to-antenna-scale ratio, and that lever fights the offset-detachment problem in the companion lesson.

USER FEEDBACK on the build of body_B scale 0.88 + arms pose B scale 0.7 dx -10 + 3 eyes psycho_light scale 0.52 tint #cfe8e0: the three-eye band was judged good and is now settled — keep count 3, scale ~0.52, a faint tint like #cfe8e0, dy ~5. Two defects were called out. (1) The arms visibly float off the body, confirming the absolute-offset problem in the companion lesson; the cheapest fix is simply to leave create_body scale at 1.0 so the fixed arm offsets still land on the body edge, and only reach for dx compensation if a smaller body is truly needed. (2) The whole monster "reads as a plain circle" — body_B is a featureless disc, and a flat dim tint plus a small eye band is not enough to break that outline, especially with no mouth or legs available to interrupt it. Do not use shape B as the default for this style. Prefer a shape whose silhouette has incident — F (long body with hair tufts) breaks the outline directly, and A (square) or D (squat oval) at least read as a deliberate form — and consider add_arms count 4 to notch the profile.

Shape F's hair tufts do NOT solve the "plain blob" silhouette problem on this style, so the shape-F suggestion in the user-feedback lesson is now corrected. The tufts are baked into the body sprite, which means they take the body's tint — under the ABYSSAL LANTERN dim core tint (#414e7a on blue) they render as the same dark indigo mass as the body and barely register against the #2d2d44 canvas. There is no way to tint them separately, since add_ tools only reach whole parts. General rule: on a dim-core body, any silhouette incident has to come from separately-tinted parts (arms, antennas), never from detail baked into the body sprite — that detail always shares the core's low value and disappears. Body scale 1.0 did fix the floating-arm defect exactly as predicted, so keep create_body scale at 1.0.

Do not use add_arms count 4 on this style — keep count 2. Tried on body_F with pose A, scale 0.8, angle 14: the two pairs are stacked only 45px apart (pairSpacing in scene.js) so at scale 0.8 they overlap into one solid teal clump per side. It does notch the profile, but it costs two principles at once. (a) Principle 1's value split weakens, because doubling the arms doubles the mid-value area until the lighter teal rivals the body and the dim core stops dominating. (b) Principle 3's angle-14 splay becomes illegible — the individual outward flare is swallowed by the clump, the same failure pose B produced in the previous build by a different route. Only count 2 with pose A has ever rendered the flare legibly. It also widens the bottom third of the silhouette, making the already-unreachable top-heavy taper worse. If more outline incident is needed, raise arm scale slightly rather than adding a second pair.

SETTLED RECIPE — shape A (square) is the correct default body for ABYSSAL LANTERN, and it resolves the user's "reads as a plain circle" complaint. Of five shapes tried it is the only one that adds silhouette incident with no side effect: B is the featureless disc that drew the complaint, F hides its own tufts under the dim core tint, E sags bottom-heavy with an empty lower void. A's corners and flat bottom supply the outline interest that lesson #10 says a dim body cannot carry itself, and its flat top edge seats the antenna bases cleanly. Full recipe: create_body blue shape A tint #414e7a scale 1.0; add_arms blue pose A count 2 tint #8fa6bd scale 0.85 angle 14; add_antennas yellow count 2 large NO tint scale 1.15 dy -15; add_eyes psycho_light count 3 tint #cfe8e0 scale 0.52 dy 5. One adjustment needed on this shape: the asymmetric tell from principle 3 goes subtle because a fixed dx -16 is diluted by the square's greater width — use dx -24 on body_A to keep the off-center antenna cluster legible.

What makes the lantern tips read as EMITTING light is warm/cool hue contrast, not value — so principle 1's rule ("lit parts stay above 0xb8 on every channel", tips brightest) measures the wrong thing and should not be trusted. Measured on the settled body_A build: the pale mint eyes (psycho_light tinted #cfe8e0) are still HIGHER in pure luminance than the untinted yellow antenna bulbs, which render as saturated mid-value orange — yet the bulbs unmistakably read as the light source, because they are the only warm element in an otherwise entirely cool composition (indigo body, teal arms, mint eyes). Practical rule: keep every part except the antennas cool, and let the antennas be the sole warm accent; that single hue contrast sells the glow even when the antennas are not the brightest thing on the canvas. Corollary — do not chase making the bulbs out-brighten the eyes by value, which earlier builds wasted effort on; just avoid adding a second warm element anywhere else.

At the settled eye scale of 0.52, psycho_light and cute_light are NOT interchangeable — always use psycho_light. The style brief lists cute_light, psycho_light and blue as equally acceptable "light-valued" styles, but that is wrong at small scale: cute_light's pupils are dark brown and occupy most of each eye once scaled to 0.52, so the three-eye band renders as three dark sockets and fails principle 4's "lit from within" requirement. psycho_light has a much smaller dark center with a wide light ring around it, which still reads as glowing at 0.52. The brief's permitted-eye-style list should be narrowed to psycho_light for this size. Note the failure is scale-dependent — cute_light's pupil ratio only becomes dominant when the sprite is shrunk, which is why it looked acceptable in an early full-size test.

Two validated ways to vary an ABYSSAL LANTERN monster so the family has more than one member without breaking any principle. (1) CORE HUE: create_body color green with the same #414e7a tint yields a dark desaturated teal-green core that is dim, cool and clearly separated from the #2d2d44 canvas — and blue-based arms tinted #8fa6bd still render clearly LIGHTER than it, so the value split survives a cross-base-color pairing (this is the check lesson #3 demands whenever base colors differ). Small caveat: green body against blue arms are two different cool hues and fragment the "one creature" read slightly, so all-blue remains the cleaner default. (2) ANTENNA COUNT: count 3 at dx -24 is better than count 2 for principle 3's asymmetric tell. The dx -24 figure predicted for body_A is confirmed — the cluster is unmistakably off-center where dx -16 had gone subtle on this wider shape. count 3 strengthens the tell further for a non-obvious reason: antennas are not placed as a mirrored pair, so all three stalks lean the same direction and that shared lean compounds the asymmetry rather than averaging it out.

Arm pose C verdict, and a general warning: the scale param is NOT comparable across arm poses, exactly as tint is not comparable across parts. Pose C's sprite is intrinsically much larger than pose A's, so add_arms scale 0.85 — correct for pose A — renders pose C as broad sweeping arcs that dominate the composition. Pose C is worth keeping as a family variant because it gives the best silhouette incident found so far: the arms bow outward and the clawed hands curl back inward, enclosing a pocket of background on each side, which directly answers the user's "reads as a plain circle" complaint without the body sprite having to carry any detail. But at 0.85 it inflates the mid-value teal area enough to weaken principle 1's dim-core dominance and it widens the bottom of the silhouette. Use pose C at scale ~0.7, not 0.85; reserve scale 0.85 for pose A. Always re-check the value balance in a screenshot after changing pose, since the pose change alone silently changes how much area the arm tint covers.

STRUCTURAL TRADE-OFF found across builds 4, 5 and 7: on this toolset, silhouette incident and principle 1's dim-core dominance are in direct conflict, because the arms are the only mid-value mass available. Every method tried for making the monster less of a plain blob works by enlarging that mid-value area, and therefore weakens the value split by the same act — add_arms count 4 did it (lesson #11), and pose C at scale 0.85 did it again (lesson #16). Only two sources of outline incident are FREE of this cost: the body shape's own outline (shape A's corners and flat bottom) and the off-center antenna cluster, because neither adds mid-value area. Practical rule: get incident from shape A plus a count-3 antenna cluster first, and treat any arm enlargement as a deliberate trade to be paid for by dropping arm scale elsewhere — do not stack arm count and arm size together. This tension is a property of having only four part tools and no legs or mouth to break the outline, so it will not go away with more parameter tuning.

USER FEEDBACK, second round — four directives that override parts of the ABYSSAL LANTERN brief. (1) Arm pose C is approved, keep it as the preferred pose over pose A. (2) Eyes must be REALISTIC: use add_eyes style "human" with a color (e.g. color blue), which renders white sclera + colored iris + pupil. This deliberately overrides principle 4's "lit from within" glow requirement and supersedes lesson #14's psycho_light preference — the user wants anatomical eyes, not abstract glowing rings. human at scale 0.52 with count 3 reads well and needs no tint. (3) The hair tufts on shape F are liked and wanted, so shape F is now preferred over shape A despite lesson #12 — but see the companion lesson, the tufts stay faint. (4) The limbs should be evenly distributed rather than bunched.

Evenly distributed limbs are NOT achievable through add_arms parameters — this is a hardcoded limit, not a tuning problem. scene.js sets pairSpacing = 45 for stacked arm pairs, so with count 4 the second pair sits only 45px below the first. A pose C arm is roughly 105px tall at scale 0.7, so the pairs always overlap into a doubled cluster per side (doubled shoulders, doubled claws); avoiding overlap would need arm scale near 0.3, which is unusably small. Within current tools the only honest choices are to accept the cluster or use count 2. Fixing it properly requires editing scene.js to expose a spacing parameter on add_arms and threading it through index.js — offer that rather than burning iterations on scale values. Related: on shape F the hair tufts the user likes are further hidden when the antenna cluster sits at dy -20 directly over the top contour, so on F push antennas to dy -10 or reduce count so the tufts stay visible.

AMENDED SETTLED RECIPE, incorporating the user's second-round directives — this build is the best balance achieved and should be the starting point for future ABYSSAL LANTERN monsters: create_body blue shape F tint #414e7a scale 1.0; add_arms blue pose C count 2 tint #8fa6bd scale 0.7 angle 14; add_antennas yellow count 3 large NO tint scale 1.15 dx -24 dy -10; add_eyes human color blue count 3 scale 0.52 dy 5. Two findings confirmed. (1) count 2 is the correct answer to the user's "distribute the limbs evenly" request within existing tools — one pose C arm per side has no doubled shoulders or claws, reads as evenly placed, and restores the legible outward splay that count 4 destroyed; it is a real fix, not a concession, though genuine four-limb spacing still needs the scene.js pairSpacing change. (2) pose C at scale 0.7 (per lesson #16) keeps the mid-value teal subordinate so principle 1's dim-core dominance survives, where scale 0.85 did not — the 0.7 figure is now verified, not just predicted.

Two verified trade-offs when honoring the user's hair and realistic-eye directives on shape F. (1) Antenna dy -10 does expose the hair tufts that dy -20 was covering — they now read at the top of the head and along the right edge, fixing the occlusion noted in lesson #19. The cost is that tucking the cluster lower removes vertical extension at the top, so it slightly weakens what little top-heaviness the silhouette had; accept this, since the user explicitly wants the hair and principle 2 is unreachable anyway. (2) add_eyes style human renders a pure white sclera and, left untinted, becomes the highest-luminance element on the canvas — the face pulls focus harder than the amber lantern bulbs. The warm/cool rule from lesson #13 still keeps the bulbs reading as the light source, so this is a matter of emphasis rather than a broken principle. Next thing to try: apply the faint cool tint #cfe8e0 to the human eyes, which should preserve the anatomical realism the user asked for while knocking the sclera back below the bulbs in emphasis — untested as of this build.

FINAL RECIPE — supersedes lesson #20, which lacked the eye tint. create_body blue shape F tint #414e7a scale 1.0; add_arms blue pose C count 2 tint #8fa6bd scale 0.7 angle 14; add_antennas yellow count 3 large NO tint scale 1.15 dx -24 dy -10; add_eyes human color blue count 3 tint #cfe8e0 scale 0.52 dy 5. The open question from lesson #21 is resolved positively: tinting the human eyes #cfe8e0 drops the sclera from pure white to pale mint WITHOUT losing the anatomical read the user asked for, and the amber bulbs regain clear focal emphasis. Status of the four principles at this recipe — (1) value split passes, cleanest of ten builds; (2) taper fails and is structurally unreachable, do not retry; (3) symmetric splay plus one off-center antenna tell passes; (4) eye band passes on the user's amended realistic terms. Further parameter iteration on this recipe re-confirms rather than discovers; the remaining improvements need code changes, namely a spacing param on add_arms and exposing add_legs/add_mouth.

Tint multiplication preserves a sprite's INTERNAL contrast structure while lowering its overall value — this is why a detailed sprite can be value-matched into a restricted palette without losing its identity. Demonstrated by tinting add_eyes style human with #cfe8e0: multiplying scales every channel proportionally, so the sclera-to-iris and iris-to-pupil contrast ratios survive intact and the eye still reads as anatomical; only the whole sprite's brightness drops. The practical consequence is that you should NOT avoid tinting a sprite out of fear of destroying its detail — reach for a faint tint whenever a detailed part is too bright for its role in the composition. The genuine limits on tint remain the ones already recorded: it can only ever darken (lesson #3), and tint numbers are not comparable across parts with different base art (lesson #3) or across arm poses for scale (lesson #16). Contrast survives; absolute brightness does not.

The "only four build tools" constraint from lesson #4 is GONE — experimental_command forwards any command name straight to scene.js's switch, so add_legs, add_mouth and clear_monster have been callable all along without ever being registered as MCP tools, and they accept the full styling param set. Verified in gallery/abyssal-lantern/014.png with experimental_command {command:"add_legs", params:{color:"blue",shape:"A",tint:"#8fa6bd",scale:0.65,dy:10,angle:-8}} and {command:"add_mouth", params:{style:"I",tint:"#6080ff",scaleX:0.7,scaleY:0.8,dy:16}}, both of which rendered correctly. Consequence: principle 2's top-heavy taper and principle 4's small low mouth — declared structurally unreachable in lessons #4, #8 and #22 — are both reachable, and 014.png is the first build in this series to satisfy all four principles at once. Stop planning around the missing tools; reach for the hatch instead. Note one caveat found while doing it: every mouth sprite is warm brown, so a mouth needs a strongly blue-weighted tint to obey lesson #13's "antennas are the only warm accent" rule, and mouth I keeps a magenta tongue that survives tinting as a violet blob — prefer a mouth style without that highlight if the second accent matters.

Lesson #17's "silhouette incident vs dim-core dominance are in direct conflict" is an artifact of arms having been the only spare part, not a structural law — legs break the trade-off. Measured on gallery/abyssal-lantern/014.png: legs and arms carry identical mid-value mass (both effective #2489a6, luminance 118 against a body at 58), yet adding legs does NOT weaken the dim core the way a second arm pair did in lesson #11, because legs extend the silhouette DOWNWARD into empty canvas instead of thickening the body's flanks where they compete with the core. Practical rule: when a monster needs outline interest, add legs rather than more or bigger arms — it buys taper and incident at once for the same mid-value cost that arms spend on neither. Companion measurement from the same build: a cool-tinted mouth is the only part that lands DARKER than the body (mouth I with tint #6080ff gives effective #1e1728, luminance 26, contrast 32 below the body), so it anchors the dark end of the value range; every build before 014 ran only from the body upward, which is why the lower body kept reading as an empty void.
